newsitem.title: USA: Grains, oil lead commodity prices lower.
newsitem.headline: Grains, oil lead commodity prices lower.

text.p: Grain prices tumbled Monday as weather improved in the Midwest, and oil and gold also fell.
The Commodity Research Bureau index of 17 futures lost 1.01 points to 245.63.

Lack of frost in the Midwest over the weekend and forecasts for warm, dry weather this week triggered heavy selling of grain contracts by speculators who had bet cold weather would hurt corn and soybean crops.

Soybeans for November delivery fell 25-1/4 cents to $7.58 a bushel and December corn ended 6-1/2 cents lower at $2.96-3/4, the lowest closing price since Jan. 29, both at the Chicago Board of Trade (CBOT).
"The weather right now is absolutely beautiful," said grain analyst Steve Bruce of E.D. and F. Man International.

Prices fell sharply on the CBOT's electronic trading system overnight after the weather improved in the Midwest and then again from the opening bell after the Department of Agriculture reported higher-than-expected supplies in its quarterly report issued on Monday morning.
The department said domestic soybean stockpiles stood 183.2 million bushels as of Sept. 1, comapred to analysts' estimates of 163 million bushels.
U.S. corn stocks were pegged at 426.3 million bushels, above analysts' estimates of 413 million bushels.
At the New York Mercantile Exchange oil prices ended lower after last week's rally. Talk that a deal to allow Iraq to sell oil may be revived fuelled selling.

November crude oil fell 22 cents to $24.38 a barrel and October unleaded gasoline fell 1.89 cents to 62.71 cents a gallon. October heating oil edged up 0.02 cent to 71.51 cents a gallon. October contracts expired on Monday.
"There was expiration-related selling in refined products, and news that the humanitarian aid for Iraq may get going took crude lower," said William Brown, president of trading firm W.H. Brown & Co.

United Nations Under-Secretary General Yasushi Akashi told a news conference in Geneva that he hoped the oil-for-food agreement could be implemented "in the near future," adding later that it might be "a matter of weeks."
Most traders dismissed Akashi's comments, saying implementation of the deal this year was highly unlikely.
But his words served to remind them that as much as 700,000 barrels a day of Iraqi oil exports could hit the market once the deal is implemented.

Oil analysts originally had expected the first Iraqi oil exports this month after Baghdad was hit by crippling U.N. sanctions in 1990. But the plan was suspended when President Saddam Hussein sent Iraqi troops into Kurdish areas in northern Iraq at the beginning of September.
At the New York Mercantile Exchange's COMEX division, precious metals ended lower as a higher dollar and the rising stock market diluted investor interest.
December gold fell $2.30 to $380.50 an ounce after falling to $380.10 during the session, a new three-year low for the December contract.

"U.S. dollar strength is depressing precious metal demand, particularly in Japan, while healthy U.S. equity and bond markets are providing no incentive for investors in precious metals either," Smith Barney analyst David Rinehimer said.
The dollar hit a 32-month high of 111.68 yen on Monday.
